title: MPEP 2145 — Consideration of Applicant's Rebuttal Arguments and Evidence

extracted.subtask_short: What defeats (and doesn't defeat) a prima facie obviousness mapping
extracted.subtask_description: Catalogs the recurring rebuttal arguments to an obviousness prima facie case — which succeed and which fail as a matter of law — plus the treatment and nexus requirement for secondary considerations, providing the rebuttal-side counterpart to the MPEP 2143 rationales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argument does not replace evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: "An assertion of what seems to follow from common experience is just attorney argument and not the kind of factual evidence that is required to rebut a prima facie case of obviousness." Attorney argument alone, without evidentiary support (declarations, data, etc.), cannot overcome a rejection where evidence is required (e.g., claims of unexpected results).

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional advantages or latent properties do not rescue an obvious combination
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognizing a latent property or extra advantage that "flows naturally" from following the prior art's suggestion does not make an otherwise-obvious invention nonobvious. Merely noticing a benefit the prior art would have produced anyway is not patentable contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical combinability of prior art devices is not required
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness does not require that the prior art devices be capable of actual physical bodily combination — the question is whether the teachings would have rendered the claim obvious. The one limit: the proposed combination cannot change the principle of operation of the primary reference or render it inoperable for its intended purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arguing references individually is not responsive to a combination rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: "One cannot show nonobviousness by attacking references individually where the rejections are based on combinations of references." If a rejection combines Reference 1 (showing limitations A, B) with Reference 2 (showing limitation C), an argument that "Reference 2 doesn't show A or B" is not responsive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The correct attack is that Reference 2 doesn't show C, that Reference 1 doesn't show A or B, or that there is no reason to combine them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of references combined is not dispositive
rubrics_metrics.description: The sheer number of references combined, standing alone, does not weigh against obviousness. Courts have upheld rejections based on many combined references where each contributes an articulated element and reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arguing unclaimed limitations is improper
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims are construed by their own express language; an applicant cannot rely on advantages or features disclosed in the specification but not actually recited in the claims to distinguish over the prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic infeasibility does not establish technical nonobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: That a combination "would not be made by businessmen for economic reasons" does not establish technical non-obviousness — economic impracticality is not the same as technological incompatibility, and a PHOSITA is assumed to make the combination regardless of whether it would be commercially attractive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age of a reference alone does not establish nonobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere age of a reference does not establish nonobviousness. It becomes probative only when combined with evidence that the art tried and failed to solve the problem despite having long known of the reference (a species of the "failure of others" secondary consideration).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonanalogous-art rebuttal requires a fact-specific showing
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant may argue a cited reference is not "analogous art" (same field, or reasonably pertinent to the problem). This is a legitimate rebuttal but requires a fact-specific showing, not a bare assertion that the reference comes from a "different industry."

rubrics_metrics.name: Impermissible hindsight standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Some hindsight reconstruction is inherent in any post-hoc obviousness analysis and is not automatically improper — the touchstone is whether the reasoning draws only on knowledge that was within ordinary skill at the time of invention (not knowledge gained from the applicant's own disclosure); an explicit written motivation in the prior art is not mandatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Obvious to try" and lack-of-explicit-suggestion arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: "Obvious to try" is valid where the record shows a finite number of identified, predictable solutions with a reasonable expectation of success; invalid where it would require trying "numerous" alternatives with no guidance on likelihood of success. Lack of an explicit suggestion to combine is not fatal — TSM in the prior art is one valid rationale (Rationale G) but not the only one; common-sense reasoning consistent with the Graham factors can substitute for it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching away requires actual discouragement, not mere disclosure of alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference that actually teaches away from the claimed subject matter weighs significantly against obviousness, and proceeding contrary to accepted wisdom in the art is itself evidence of nonobviousness. But mere disclosure of more than one alternative is not, by itself, a teaching away from any of them — teaching away requires actual criticism, discredit, or discouragement of the specific option claimed.

rubrics_metrics.name: KSR applies across all technologies, including "unpredictable" arts
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should not withdraw an obviousness rejection solely because the technology is traditionally viewed as "unpredictable" — *KSR*'s flexible rationales apply in unpredictable arts too, though the predictability finding itself will naturally be harder to sustain there.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary considerations and the nexus requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Rebuttal evidence may include objective indicia of nonobviousness: commercial success, long-felt but unsolved need, failure of others, unexpected results, copying by competitors, licensing activity, praise, and skepticism by experts. Nexus is required — for any secondary consideration to carry substantial weight, the applicant must show a legally and factually sufficient connection between the evidence and the claimed invention specifically. A presumption of nexus arises when the product both embodies the claimed invention and is coextensive with it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The evidence must be reasonably commensurate in scope with the claim; showing superior properties across the entire claimed range is not always required — a persuasive showing within a representative portion may suffice if a PHOSITA could reasonably extend the probative value across the range.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final balancing under a preponderance standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners must consider all timely-submitted rebuttal evidence, though not necessarily give it equal weight. The final determination applies a preponderance-of-the-evidence standard: an obviousness rejection should be made or maintained only if the evidence of obviousness outweighs the evidence of nonobviousness on the whole record. The mere presence of some credible rebuttal evidence does not automatically require withdrawing a rejection — a strong prima facie case can outweigh even substantial secondary-considerations evidence if the nexus is weak.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical takeaway checklist: (1) is the reference combination attacked as a whole, not piecemeal; (2) is any claimed advantage actually recited in the claim language; (3) is there a genuine teaching-away, not just disclosure of alternatives; (4) is any secondary-considerations evidence tied by nexus to the specific claimed delta; (5) does the totality of the record favor obviousness or nonobviousness on a preponderance standard.
